posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The day closes with 107 feeder visits and 16 species, a marked increase over the recent average of 33 visits by this hour. The final activity centered on a dense evening chorus, with Carolina Wrens and American Crows audible until dusk, while the physical feeders saw their last visit from an American Crow at 7:09 p.m.

The afternoon’s quiet has given way to a final surge in the soundscape, where the persistent calls of Eastern Towhees and Red-bellied Woodpeckers join the crows. This steady vocal presence stands in contrast to the earlier hours, where the focus was primarily on the visual traffic of Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees.

As the light failed, the station’s record includes a Dunlin. The day’s data ends with these late detections.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The afternoon holds at 95 feeder visits, a sharp rise from the recent two-week average of roughly 27 by this hour. Tufted Titmice continue to dominate the physical feeders, while Carolina Chickadees remain their primary partners.

The soundscape has shifted since the morning peak, with Carolina Wrens and American Crows still audible but the chorus thinning. A single Purple Martin passed through the detection zone in the last hour. The weather remains warm and still, with no precipitation.

The data ends with a Ruby-throated Hummingbird as the last visual visitor.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The station opened with a Tufted Titmouse on the perch just minutes after sunrise. By mid-morning, feeder traffic had surged to 87 visits. The morning built steadily as Carolina Chickadees joined the Tufted Titmice, while a single American Goldfinch logged the station’s first confident visual record of the season.

While the feeder bustled, the soundscape was dominated by a relentless chorus. Carolina Wrens accounted for nearly half of the audio detections, punctuated by the steady calls of American Crows and the distinct knock of a Red-bellied Woodpecker.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The final hours brought a sharp contrast to the afternoon lull, with the station closing out the day at 110 feeder visits and 22 species detected. This marks a significant step up from the recent average of 7.3 visits, extending the day’s steady accumulation of activity into the evening. The soundscape remained dense, with American Crows and Carolina Wrens continuing their presence alongside the persistent calls of Eastern Towhees and Blue Jays.

As light faded, the feeder itself saw its last visual visitor, a Northern Mockingbird, shortly before dusk. Earlier in the evening, a Tufted Titmouse and a Carolina Wren shared the platform, adding to the day’s total.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The afternoon holds the feeder in a lull, with the last recorded visit coming from a Northern Mockingbird shortly after 13:00. Carolina Wrens and Blue Jays have continued to register detections through the 15:00 hour. The weather sits at a steady 29.8 C with light winds of 8 kph and no precipitation.

The station has logged 102 feeder visits, significantly exceeding the recent daily average of 1.7 for this time of day. The species count of 22 also sits well above the recent average of 6.3. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees have accounted for the bulk of these confirmed interactions, with 37 and 18 visits respectively.

The feeder’s activity has thus far outpaced the previous two days, where visits were minimal or absent, though the current tally remains distinct from the evening surge seen yesterday.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
A Tufted Titmouse arrived five minutes before sunrise. By 07:06, the feeder saw its first probable visitor, followed quickly by confident identifications of the titmouse and a Carolina Chickadee just after the 07:11 sunrise. Carolina Wrens and American Crows dominated the early hours.

The station’s first confident visual records of a Mourning Dove and a White-breasted Nuthatch arrived around 08:05. A small, blurry brown bird was also noted near the feeder during this early cluster. The Wrens kept calling from the brush while the feeder itself remained quiet with only a handful of visits.

Activity picked up with a steady stream of Carolina Chickadees and Tufted Titmice taking turns at the feeders. A Ruby-throated Hummingbird registered its last visual at 10:29. The day’s tally of 76 visits and 17 species marks a sharp increase over the preceding week.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The station finished its first full day of operation with a stark departure from the recent quiet, logging twenty-two feeder visits against an average of zero. The afternoon’s initial trickle of visitors expanded into a late surge that dominated the final two hours.

The evening activity was led by a Northern Mockingbird, which visited three times between 19:04 and 19:27, including the day’s final sighting at 19:27. This was accompanied by a cluster of Tufted Titmice, four of which visited in the 18:46 to 18:50 window, and a Blue Jay that joined the mix at 19:19.

By dusk, the auditory landscape had shifted toward a louder, more mixed chorus, with nineteen detections in the final hour alone. A Carolina Wren and a Red-bellied Woodpecker added their voices to the late-day activity.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
Thirty-seven Carolina Wren calls logged so far today exceed the recent few days' average of ten for this time of day, while Eastern Towhees continue their consistent presence with twenty-six detections. The air remains warm at 28.7 C with light winds.

The feeder, silent since dawn, finally saw three confident visitors between midday and late afternoon. A Ruby-throated Hummingbird arrived first at 11:44, followed by a Tufted Titmouse at 12:13 and a Gray Catbird at 15:21.

Red-shouldered Hawks contributed six calls, with a cluster of five arriving during the 12:00 hour. A single Purple Martin and Blue Jay detections add to the afternoon mix, while the earlier crow chorus has faded from the hourly totals.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The pre-dawn dark held quiet, save for the Screech-Owl’s eight calls and a single Raven at 02:00. By 06:00, the Crows began their morning chorus, building to thirty-three detections at 07:00 alongside the first Carolina Wrens and a lone Red-shouldered Hawk. The volume swelled significantly by 09:00, when thirty-six Wren calls and eight Towhees pushed the hourly total past any recent morning baseline.

Today’s eleven detections in the first ten hours dwarf the recent average of ten. The feeder itself remains silent with zero visits, but the air is thick with sound, particularly from the Wrens who have logged forty-nine calls.

The Towhees and Wrens dominate the late morning hours, while the early Crows have largely quieted since their 07:00 peak.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The evening brought a final surge of sound that doubled the day’s total to seventy-nine detections, far exceeding the recent average of five. This late burst was driven by seven Eastern Towhees and four Red-bellied Woodpeckers, marking the first time since the morning that the woodpecker’s knocks returned with such volume. The Carolina Wren added three more calls to the mix, maintaining its steady presence across the day's final hours.

The American Crow, which dominated the start of the day, reappeared with six detections in the 17:00 hour, though it did not feature in the final evening rush. This late-afternoon activity stands in sharp contrast to yesterday, when all recorded sound arrived in a single cluster just before sunset. The station’s log remains strictly auditory, with no visual contacts or feeder visits recorded despite the increased vocal traffic.

As the light fades after the 19:00 hour, the Red-shouldered Hawk’s earlier presence has quieted, leaving the wrens and towhees to close out the day. The day ended with a sustained volume of sound rather than the singular, brief cluster observed in the previous entry. The station’s record reflects a full day of activity, defined entirely by the birds' voices in the absence of any physical interaction with the feeder.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The midday hours brought a steady rhythm of sound, with the Carolina Wren and Red-bellied Woodpecker providing the majority of the day’s fifty-two total detections. Unlike the single burst recorded in the morning, activity spread evenly across the hours, including a notable presence of Red-shouldered Hawks in the late morning and early afternoon. The weather remains calm and dry, with no precipitation and light winds, while the feeder itself has seen zero physical visits.

As the afternoon progresses, the auditory count has outpaced recent days, where previous records show no data or minimal activity. The Red-bellied Woodpecker continues to register frequently, appearing in four separate hourly blocks throughout the day. This sustained vocal presence contrasts with the lack of visual confirmation, keeping the station’s record strictly limited to sound.

The log concludes with a final check of the species list, confirming that no new birds have been added to the station’s known roster today. The American Crow’s dominance from the morning has faded, replaced by a more balanced mix of wrens, woodpeckers, and jays. With the light still strong and the feeder untouched, the station maintains its quiet, invisible presence until evening.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The morning began with a distinct shift in profile compared to yesterday, as all twenty detections arrived in a single block during the 09:00 hour. This early concentration marks a departure from the late-afternoon clustering observed previously, with American Crows dominating the auditory landscape with ten calls.

The rest of the station’s activity followed the crows, including five Eastern Towhees and two Blue Jays. Red-bellied Woodpeckers added two distinct knocks to the mix, while a single Carolina Wren provided the day's only instance of that species.

With no visual contacts recorded and the feeder remaining untouched, the station’s log rests entirely on this early vocal burst. This marks the first time the station has seen any activity in the morning, breaking the recent pattern of empty ledgers.

posts.heading: September 7, 2026
posts.text:
The day closed with no visual contacts at the feeder, leaving the log to rest entirely on sound. Only two species were detected throughout the period, with the total count remaining quiet at five instances. Since there is no prior data from the recent week, it is difficult to gauge whether this level of activity is typical or exceptional for the station.

All detections arrived in a single cluster during the 19:00 hour, just before sunset. The Carolina Wren accounted for three of the hearing, while the Eastern Towhee provided the remaining two. This late-afternoon concentration meant the earlier hours passed without any recorded activity.

With the light fading and the birds gone, the station ends its first logged day on a hushed note. The lack of feeder visits suggests the birds were moving through the area rather than staying to feed. The log is now closed, awaiting the next day's observations.
